final_proof:
We prove the identity by Fejér summation, including the convergence fact that is needed.

Lemma (Fejér). If g is a continuous 2π-periodic function and

a₀=(1/π)∫_{-π}^{π}g(t)dt,   a_n=(1/π)∫_{-π}^{π}g(t)cos(nt)dt,   b_n=(1/π)∫_{-π}^{π}g(t)sin(nt)dt,

then its Fejér means

σ_N(g,x)=a₀/2+Σ_{n=1}^N(1-n/(N+1))(a_n cos(nx)+b_n sin(nx))

converge uniformly to g(x).

Proof of the lemma. Put

K_N(t)=1+2Σ_{n=1}^N(1-n/(N+1))cos(nt).

Averaging the finite Dirichlet kernels (or summing a finite geometric progression) gives

K_N(t)=1/(N+1)·(sin((N+1)t/2)/sin(t/2))²

for t not a multiple of 2π, with the value at such a multiple defined by continuity. Thus K_N≥0. Also, integration of its finite cosine expansion gives ∫_{-π}^{π}K_N(t)dt=2π. Direct substitution of the Fourier coefficients into the finite sum, followed by the elementary angle-addition identities, gives

σ_N(g,x)=(1/(2π))∫_{-π}^{π}g(x-t)K_N(t)dt.

For every fixed δ with 0<δ<π and δ≤|t|≤π,

K_N(t)≤1/((N+1)sin²(δ/2)).

Because a continuous periodic function is uniformly continuous on the circle, given ε>0 we may choose δ so that |g(x-t)-g(x)|<ε whenever |t|<δ, uniformly in x. If M=max|g|, then the convolution formula, the nonnegativity and normalization of K_N, and the preceding bound show

|σ_N(g,x)-g(x)|≤ε+(1/(2π))∫_{δ≤|t|≤π}2M K_N(t)dt
≤ε+2M/((N+1)sin²(δ/2)).

The second term tends to zero uniformly in x. Since ε was arbitrary, σ_N(g,·) converges uniformly to g. This proves the lemma.

Now let f(x)=x² for -π≤x≤π and extend f with period 2π. The endpoint values agree, so this periodic extension is continuous and the lemma applies. Since f is even, b_n=0 for every n. Moreover,

a₀=(2/π)∫_0^π x²dx=2π²/3.

For n≥1, integration by parts twice yields

∫_0^π x²cos(nx)dx=[x²sin(nx)/n]_0^π-(2/n)∫_0^π x sin(nx)dx
=-(2/n)([-x cos(nx)/n]_0^π+(1/n)∫_0^π cos(nx)dx)
=2π(-1)^n/n².

Consequently

a_n=(2/π)∫_0^π x²cos(nx)dx=4(-1)^n/n².

Evaluate the Fejér means at x=π. Since cos(nπ)=(-1)^n, the lemma gives

π²=f(π)=lim_{N→∞}σ_N(f,π)
=π²/3+4 lim_{N→∞}Σ_{n=1}^N(1-n/(N+1))/n².

It remains only to identify the last limit with the ordinary sum. The series Σ_{n=1}^∞1/n² converges, since for n≥2,

1/n²≤1/(n(n-1))=1/(n-1)-1/n.

Writing H_N=Σ_{n=1}^N1/n, we have

Σ_{n=1}^N(1-n/(N+1))/n²=Σ_{n=1}^N1/n²-H_N/(N+1).

Furthermore H_N≤1+log N, so H_N/(N+1)→0. Hence the weighted sums tend to Σ_{n=1}^∞1/n². Therefore

π²=π²/3+4Σ_{n=1}^∞1/n²,

and rearranging gives

ζ(2)=Σ_{n=1}^∞1/n²=π²/6.
